items.correction: The facts hold; two parts needed correcting. (1) Severity: P1, as the adversarial reviewer filed it, is too high. No promise the spec states becomes false. The Goal (lines 20-21) promises 'without sending the score, its file name, its track names or the music', and section 5 (lines 252-253) promises that every field is a fixed value or a number; a size in whole KB breaks neither. P2 fits (see the severity note). (2) The adversarial fix, 'bytes rounded up to a power of two, in KB', gives fractions of a KB for files under 1 KB (32 bytes would be 0.03125 KB). Rounding the size in whole KB up to a power of two with the same function, roundedSize(Math.ceil(bytes / 1024)), gives exactly Sentry's rounded bytes divided by 1024 for every file over 1 KB (checked by a scratch script), keeps whole numbers, and still tells an empty file (0) from a tiny one (1). Also, roundedSize() is private inside report.ts in the Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), so the move must export it.

items.central_claim_check: Checked four things. (1) The Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), 'Choices this plan makes', Choice 3 (how the file's type and size travel): bytes is 'rounded up to the next power of two (0 stays 0), where the spec sent the exact count: an exact size and the type together could single out a widely shared file, and nothing needs the exact number. Approved in the plan review, lap 1.' Its table of questions repeats the decision, and its report.ts sketch (its Task 5, the reporting functions) holds the function, roundedSize(), private, with the comment 'so the type and an exact size cannot single out one widely shared file'. The plan commit that added it, df7e287b ('sizes round up', 2026-10-09), is later than this spec's round 1 (first commits 2026-10-08), as the adversarial reviewer says. (2) This spec sends file_size_kb 'rounded to whole KB' (line 274) on open_file, each time a visitor opens their own file (line 258), and on score_failed (line 260); it is typed at line 291 and registered as a metric in setup step 4 (line 403). The same visit sends file_type, track_count and instruments (line 259) under Google's visitor-ID cookie _ga (line 360), kept 14 months (setup step 2, line 391). (3) No goal needs the exact size. 'Why this exists' (lines 48-51) asks who comes, what they use and where they stop; the bonus for NH-52 (the service-level-objective ticket that wants a failure rate), at lines 326-327, needs only counts of open_file and score_failed. (4) Reasoned, not tested: whether anyone could in practice match a size to a known shared file. The numbers: today's rule can send 25,601 different sizes up to the 25 MB open limit (web/app/play/OpenFileControl.tsx:26); the rounded rule can send 17.

spike.what: A scratch Node script copies roundedSize() from the Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request). For every 97th byte count from 1 KB to 64 MB, and for every power of two plus and minus one, it compares roundedSize(Math.ceil(bytes / 1024)) with roundedSize(bytes) / 1024. Then it prints today's rule and the rounded rule for the Sentry plan's own test sizes, and counts the different values each rule can send up to the 25 MB limit.
spike.result: Equal for every size above 1 KB, with no mismatch. 0 bytes gives 0 KB; 1, 5 and 32 bytes give 1 KB (today's whole-KB rule sends 0 for them, the same as for an empty file); 48,213 bytes gives 64 KB (today 47); 25 MB gives 32,768 KB (today 25,600). Up to the limit: 25,601 possible values today, 17 when rounded.

items.scenario: You download a popular drum tab — the same file thousands of drummers share — and open it in Notation Hero. Google Analytics receives its type, its size to the kilobyte (47 KB), its five tracks and its instruments, filed under the visitor ID it keeps in a cookie. Anyone who can read the reports, and who has the same file, can tell that this visitor plays that song. When a file fails to open, Sentry receives only '64 KB or less' — the rounding approved for Sentry for exactly this reason.
items.whats_wrong: Section 5 sends Google the file size rounded to whole KB (line 274), on every open of a visitor's own file and on every failed open. The Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), approved after this spec was written, rounds the same fact up to a power of two, because an exact size and the type 'could single out a widely shared file'. So Google, which keeps a visitor ID, gets the finer number, beside the track count and the instruments, while Sentry, which keeps none, gets the coarser one. The spec gives no reason for the difference, and no goal needs the exact size.

Text rows report only on blur or Enter (SettingRow.tsx:174-195) and sliders once per drag (SliderDraft.ts), as the spec expects.
items.contradicts: none. Checked the intro rule (line 253), which the fix extends rather than replaces; the 'Not client/' non-goal (line 38), kept, since the settling lives in web/lib/analytics/; section 4's track() bullet (lines 232-235: nothing before the start, only declared keys), which the held event still passes through; round 1's change that makes track() send only the declared fields (commit 70b4a9e0), which the settle step sits in front of; section 9's track() unit test (lines 433-434), extended; and the rule for NH-349 (the 'Privacy choices' link that lets a visitor change an answer) that no hit follows a 'No' (lines 507-512), kept because the held event goes through track().

spike.what: Two spikes. (1) A scratch Node test runs a settle helper under Node's fake timers: it keeps the latest fields per key (the event name, plus the setting key) and sends them 1 second after the last change, or at once on pagehide; the call sites skip an unchanged value. (2) A scratch Playwright script in the installed Chromium 149 (Playwright 1.61.1 from web/): a local page queues the spec's consent default, settings, js and config through a gtag() function kept local to the page's script, never put on window; then, after the load event, it adds Google's real gtag.js, served from a copy fetched once from Google's public address with a made-up ID. Every request to a Google host was answered locally (204), and Chromium's resolver also mapped every Google host to 'not found', so nothing could reach Google; the script counted requests seen against requests answered, and they matched in every run. In it, the page holds one tempo_change in the helper and is then left by a navigation, with the helper flushing on pagehide, on the change to hidden, on both, or not at all.
spike.result: (1) All 7 cases pass. A held + button (40 steps at 60 ms) sends one tempo_change with speed 140 %; typing 1, 15, 150 and then leaving the box 3 s later sends one setting_change; tabbing past a box sends none; a 30-move colour drag sends one; two rows edited in turn send one each; pagehide in the middle of a burst sends the held event at once, and only once; without the helper the same hold sends 40. (2) With no flush, the held event was lost on navigation; flushing on pagehide or on the change to hidden delivered it (on a same-tab navigation Chromium fired pagehide first). A tab close could not be observed in this harness — no hit at all arrived after a close, not even Google's own — so that case is (untested).

items.scenario: You hold the + button on the tempo control to go from 100 to 140 BPM. Google Analytics records forty tempo changes, one per step. Then you type 150 into a number box in Settings and press Tab: four 'setting changed' events — one per digit, and one more as you leave the box. A keyboard user who only tabs past ten number boxes sends up to ten, without changing anything. The report says visitors change the tempo and the settings far more often than they do.
items.whats_wrong: The spec's only guard against bursts, 'Sliders send their final value only' (line 253), does not cover the controls that send most of them. The header's tempo control reports every step of a held button (every 60 ms), every wheel notch and every typed digit. The Settings number boxes (36 number rows, plus the box beside each of the 5 sliders) report every keystroke, and again on leaving the box, even unchanged. The 6 colour rows report every move of the picker. With one track() at each call site (line 105), tempo_change and setting_change count ticks and keystrokes, not edits.

items.proposed_fix: Send tempo_change and setting_change through a settle step in web/lib/analytics/ that keeps the latest fields per control (the event name, plus the setting key) and sends them once: 1 second after the last change, or at once when the page turns hidden or is left. items.why_it_works: Every source of bursts — a held button, the wheel, typing, a picker drag, focus leaving a box — ends with at least 1 second without changes, the same time TempoControl itself uses to decide that an edit is over, so each edit becomes one event with its final value. Flushing when the page turns hidden keeps the last edit on phones, where pagehide may never fire, and sending through track() keeps the answer rules in one place.
items.clear_fix: no — it changes what Google receives (one event per edit, up to 1 second later). There is no competing option, so the only question is whether to apply it.

items.section_heading: ## 9. Testing; ## 8. Setup — done by leocaseiro, by hand
items.central_claim_check: Confirmed. Section 9 checks open_file, score_loaded and play (the Sydney case, lines 451-454) and the two mixer_change events (the Privacy case, lines 461-466); setup step 6 checks page views, open_file and score_loaded by hand (lines 406-409). That leaves seven of the eleven typed events with no check: score_failed, loop_toggle, metronome_toggle, count_in_toggle, tempo_change, setting_change and export_score — though Goal 2 ('what they use', line 49) names loop and tempo. The trap is real: web/app/play/TracksPopover.tsx:266-279 re-applies the mute and solo of every row that has one (and its volume and audio transposition) on each playerReady, which 're-fires on every MIDI reload and every player swap' (its own comment), and Solo all and Mute all call the same applySolo and applyMute once per track (422-429). A track() inside applyMute or applySolo would report presses nobody made, and one solo per track instead of one solo_all. web/e2e/player.e2e.ts already forces an E103 (the file is not a score) with a buffer that is not a score (line 574), so a score_failed check costs little.
items.contradicts: none — the suggested case adds to section 9 and changes no existing case; checked the Sydney and Privacy cases, the fixture rules (lines 440-449) and setup step 6.

spike.why: A missing test, not a claim to measure; the code it rests on was read (see the claim check).

items.scenario: A month after launch you open Google Analytics and see that nobody has ever pressed Loop. The real reason: the loop event was wired to a place that never runs. Or the reverse: each time a sound setting rebuilds the player, it re-applies every track's Solo, and an event placed there reports Solo presses nobody made. No test catches either, so you draw the wrong conclusion about what drummers use.
items.summary: True. Four of the eleven typed events have a check; seven have none, including loop and tempo, which Goal 2 ('what they use') names. A call in the wrong place either reads as 'nobody uses it' or invents use, because the mixer re-applies every Solo and Mute each time the player reloads. One end-to-end case that uses each remaining control once and counts the events in window.dataLayer would catch both, with steps the suite already has (a file that is not a score, the Solo button).
items.whats_wrong: Seven of the eleven typed events have no automated or hand check, so a call wired to the wrong place would ship unseen and make the reports wrong.

opening a fixture; `play` after pressing ▶.
(absent — no case checks score_failed, loop_toggle, metronome_toggle, count_in_toggle, tempo_change,

opening a fixture; `play` after pressing ▶.
- **Every control once:** in Sydney, open a file that is not a score, then a fixture. Press Loop,

  rebuilds the sound; export MIDI. `window.dataLayer` then holds one `score_failed` with `E103`,
  and exactly one event for each control, with its fields. The rebuild reloads the player, which
  re-applies the Solo; it adds no second `mixer_change`.

items.proposed_fix: Optional: add one end-to-end case to section 9 that uses each untested control once and checks that window.dataLayer holds exactly one event for each, including after a player reload.
items.why_it_works: Each event's call site is then proven to fire once per real action — not never, and not again when the player re-applies its state.
items.clear_fix: no — it adds a test case (scope), though a small one.
